title: The four elements
hookLine: hardness, fluid, heat, motion: the body as four. but are the four real?
tomorrow: which four thoughts could go out the door with you every morning?

cards: What is your body actually made of? A chemistry class hands you a chart of elements. Buddhaghosa hands you four, and they aren't chemistry.
They're things you can feel from the inside, right now: something hard, something fluid, something warm, something moving. Earth, water, fire, air. The practice is to look at the body as only that.
And Buddhist thinkers have disagreed over one question: are the four themselves real?

teach.b: It starts with the Buddha's advice to his son Rahula. Whatever in you is hard and solid, hair, nails, teeth, bones, is the earth element. Whatever is fluid, blood, sweat, tears, is water.
Whatever warms you and digests your food is fire. Whatever moves, the breath going in and out, is air.

teach.h: NOT MINE, NOT ME, NOT MY SELF.
teach.b: And each one, he says, is to be seen as it is: this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Buddhaghosa turns it into a meditation subject, with a short method for quick minds and a long one for the rest of us.
In the Theravada Abhidhamma, the analysis bottoms out in basic qualities like these: hardness is really there when you press your palm down, and seeing it plainly is what loosens the grip of me.

teach.h: NAGARJUNA: NONE HAS A FIXED BEING.
teach.b: Nagarjuna, the Mahayana philosopher, examines the elements in his Middle Way verses, takes space as his example, and says the others go the same way: none has a fixed being of its own.
Even earth is only earth next to what it isn't. Each side has a strong case. One says you need something solid to stand on while you let go.
The other says that if you grip the four as things, you've only traded one self for four.

how: In Theravada practice the defining of the four elements is a meditation subject in the Visuddhimagga, done by a brief or a detailed method; Mahayana students meet the elements again in Nagarjuna's analysis of emptiness.

o: four guardian spirits that protect your body
an old theory of chemistry from before atoms
the body felt as hardness, fluid, heat and motion

games.q: the four, as you feel them — tap the pairs.
p: motion: the breath in and out

s: the four elements are an early chemistry of the body
they're qualities you feel from the inside: hardness, fluid, warmth and motion, seen as not mine.
the Buddha taught this analysis to his own son
in his advice to Rahula: each element seen as it is, not mine, not me, not my self.
every Buddhist school agrees the elements are ultimately real
the Abhidhamma treats such qualities as real; Nagarjuna argues none has a fixed being of its own.

games.q: your friend says the Abhidhamma view is naive: "hardness is just a word." give the Abhidhamma side its best case.
o: it's settled because an old book says so.
hardness is felt, not invented; you need something real to see.
it was the best science anyone had back then.
games.why: its strongest point: the hardness under your palm is there whether you name it or not, and seeing it plainly loosens the grip of me. Nagarjuna's side answers that gripping the four as things just trades one self for four.

practice: Press one palm against your leg and feel the hardness: earth. Notice the wet of your mouth: water. The warmth where your hands rest: fire.
The breath moving in and out: air. Go round the four slowly, naming each one under your breath.

wordCard.voice: The four elements: earth, water, fire, air, felt as hardness, fluid, warmth and motion. Rahula heard them first, from his father.

orig.note: Pali: the defining of the four elements, this subject's name in the Visuddhimagga.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: four elements, and not one of them signed with your name. Thirty-eight of forty.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 62, Maharahulovada Sutta (the earth, water, fire and air elements within: hair, nails, teeth, bones; bile, blood, sweat, tears; what warms and digests; the in-breath and out-breath; each to be seen as it is: this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self)
